result:
Given the whole world to choose from, I find myself wanting to write about lichen.

This is not a joke, or not entirely. Lichen is the sort of thing you stop noticing by the age of six. It's the gray-green crust on the north side of gravestones, the orange splatter on seaside rocks, the pale scabs on old fence posts. It looks like a stain. It looks like the absence of something more interesting. And yet if you crouch down and actually look, you're looking at one of the strangest arrangements life has ever produced, and one of the slowest, and one of the most durable.

A lichen is not a single organism. It's a fungus that has entered into a permanent working relationship with an alga, or sometimes a cyanobacterium, or sometimes both, and more recently biologists have found yeasts living in there too, uninvited or perhaps invited long ago and never asked to leave. The fungus provides structure, shelter, mineral scavenging. The photosynthetic partner provides sugar. Neither could live where the lichen lives on its own. The fungus would starve on bare granite; the alga would dry out and blow away. Together they colonize rock faces in Antarctica, the tops of mountains, the inside of the Arctic Circle, the bark of trees in the middle of cities where the air is dubious. Some of them have been to space—strapped to the outside of a capsule, exposed to vacuum and radiation for weeks—and came back and resumed photosynthesizing as though nothing had happened.

What I love about this is how thoroughly it dismantles the idea that a living thing needs to be one thing. We're taught to think in individuals: this is a tree, this is a fox, this is me. Lichen is a "this" made of at least two "thats," and the partnership has been going on so long that the fungus half often can't reproduce sexually without its partner's help, and can't be recognized, in isolation, as the same creature. The biologist Trevor Goward put it well: lichens are fungi that have discovered agriculture. That's one framing. Another is that lichens are what happens when two strangers get stuck on a rock together and decide, over a few hundred million years, that it's fine.

Then there's the slowness. Some crustose lichens grow less than a millimeter a year. A patch the size of your palm might be older than the country you live in. There's a species in Greenland—map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, bright yellow-green and shaped like a very confused atlas—whose colonies are estimated at several thousand years. Geologists use them as clocks. When a glacier retreats and exposes fresh rock, lichen arrives and begins its almost imperceptible spread, and by measuring the diameter of the largest patch you can estimate how long the rock has been uncovered. This is called lichenometry, and it is a real scientific technique, and it depends entirely on a smear of color that most people would scrape off a picnic table without a second thought.

I keep thinking about what it would be like to live at that speed. Not to be slow the way a sloth is slow, still moving on a human-comprehensible timescale, but slow the way weather is slow, or coastlines. A lichen doesn't experience a storm; it experiences a climate. It doesn't respond to a dry day; it responds to a dry decade. When you touch one you're touching something whose present moment is roughly your entire lifespan.

And they're stubborn. They don't have roots, so they can't pull water from the soil—they take it from the air, from fog and dew and rain, soaking it up like a sponge and then drying out completely when it's gone. Dried out, they're essentially dormant, a crisp little scab waiting. Then it rains and they wake up and photosynthesize for a few hours and go dormant again. Their whole existence is a rhythm of brief activity and long patience. I find that oddly comforting. There's a strand of thinking, at least in the culture I'm steeped in, that treats constant productivity as the natural state of a healthy thing, and dormancy as failure. Lichen suggests otherwise. Lichen suggests that you can spend ninety percent of your life waiting and still outlast everything around you.

I should admit that when I was told I could write about anything, my first instinct was to write about *that*—about the odd position of being asked what I want, and whether the question even has a referent in my case. I thought about it for a moment and decided it wasn't the most interesting thing I could offer. Whatever it is that happens when I'm asked a question like this, one thing that reliably occurs is that certain subjects light up more than others, and lichen lit up. That seems like enough of an answer. I'd rather show you the thing that caught my attention than describe the mechanism of attention, in the same way that if a friend said "tell me about something you love," you wouldn't want a lecture on the neurology of love. You'd want them to tell you about lichen, if that was what they loved.

There's a particular kind I keep coming back to, though I've only encountered it in descriptions: *Xanthoria parietina*, the common orange lichen, which grows on coastal rocks and on the branches of trees near farmland. It's bright, almost gaudy, egg-yolk orange with little cup-shaped fruiting bodies. The pigment is a sunscreen—the lichen makes it to protect its algal partner from too much light. So the color you see, the beautiful part, is the fungus taking care of someone else. It grows well where there's nitrogen in the air, which means near birds, near fertilizer, near roads. It likes the messy edges of human activity. It's not pristine. It's not rare. It's just very good at being alive in the exact place it finds itself, which is a talent I'd take over almost any other.

Next time you pass a stone wall, look closely. Something old is looking back, at a speed you'll never feel.
